title: Leave, regret, resolve (2:2)
hookLine: leave the wrong, put it out of your thoughts, regret it, resolve for the future
tomorrow: so can you say sorry while still holding on to it?

cards: The kitchen is quiet now. The sentence is out, the one that was meant to sting, and it did. The person who heard it is rinsing a mug that's already clean, back turned.

And the next ten seconds go the usual way: a hand reaches for the apology. Say sorry fast, get it over with, let the room breathe again. Maimonides, writing his Laws of Return, would ask for one beat of patience here.
Not because sorry is wrong. Because in his list, sorry doesn't come first.

teach.b: In chapter two he asks a plain question: what is teshuvah, return? His answer is a short list, and the order is the lesson. First, the person leaves the wrong.

Stops doing it, and also puts it out of his thoughts, so it isn't still running in the background. For this he reaches for Isaiah: "Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts." Not only the way.
He looks back and is sorry for what happened, and here Maimonides quotes Jeremiah: "Surely after that I was turned, I repented." In that verse the turning comes first and the ache follows.
Third, resolve. He decides in his heart not to do it again, and Maimonides adds a startling detail: the One who knows what's hidden can vouch that he won't go back to it.
The resolve has to be real enough to hold up under that gaze.
Only after all three, he says, does the person confess in words, saying out loud what was already settled inside. So the apology isn't the opening move.
It's the report, the voice at the end of work the heart has already done.
Leave, regret, resolve, and then speak.

how: Some Jews study Maimonides' Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) in the season before Yom Kippur, and the confession prayers of that day name wrongs aloud.

o: walking away from someone who hurt you
a farewell blessing said when parting
stopping a wrong, even in your thoughts, first

games.q: the steps of return — tap the pairs.
p: stop it, and stop replaying it
decide in your heart: not again
say out loud what was settled

s: in Maimonides' order the words come last: leave, regret, resolve, then say it.
Maimonides asks a person to leave a wrong even in their thoughts
he cites Isaiah: forsake his way, and his thoughts.
feeling bad about it is the whole of return
regret is one step of three; resolve not to repeat it, then put it in words.

games.q: your roommate keeps borrowing your charger without asking. she texts 'sorry!!' while it's still plugged into her laptop. by Maimonides' order, what's missing?
o: the leaving: the charger's still in her laptop, so the sorry comes early.
nothing at all; she said sorry, and that completes the return.
more feeling; a longer, sadder text would make the return whole.
games.why: Maimonides puts leaving the wrong first and the words last. a sorry while still doing it skips the first step.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Choose one small wrong from this week and write three words down the page: leave, regret, resolve. Beside each, one honest phrase: what you'll stop, what you're sorry for, what you'll do next time.
Then set the pen down and sit with the page for the rest of the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Leave: the first step of return in Maimonides' list. Stop the wrong, and stop replaying it, before regret, resolve and words.

orig.note: Hebrew: return, turning back; the name of Maimonides' Laws of Return.

carryVoice: Your line: leave, regret, resolve. The words come after, and they carry more weight for the wait. Day fifteen forty-one, done.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:2 (leaving, regret, resolve, then confession)
